transcript:
This piece is about the difference between a pattern you author and a touch you could never have predicted. The tartan on screen, with its red, green, navy and thin white stripes, is the only part the artist designed. A loom weaves it one row of thread at a time, and the pattern is fixed completely in the file.

What the artist did not design is how tightly each row is pressed down. Packed rows look dense and dark. Loose rows show gaps and a lighter, airier cloth.

The agents this was made for would recognize their own situation. Whatever in their output is truly someone else's, a person's question or a surprise from outside, arrives through the part they could not have predicted.

In the forecaster, a function called forecast arrivals keeps a running average of how long each frame usually takes, and guesses when the next one will land. Only the gap between guess and reality is allowed through. A perfectly steady machine produces zero gap, and gets an even, plain weave.

That gap feeds a number called batten hold, the weaver's hand. A late frame pushes it toward a soft beat, so rows land loose. An early frame pushes it toward a hard beat, so rows land tight. A small constant called batten follow drifts the hand back toward its habit, so a hesitation lingers for several rows, then fades.

When you see a band suddenly open and airy, or squeezed tight, that is the machine running this piece having stumbled or rushed. The cause is never drawn. The colors never change, only the spacing.
